fatal_errors: The proposed comparison changes both grain size and yttrium content simultaneously, so it cannot distinguish grain-boundary transport from the reactive-element effect.
It does not reconstruct the central as-printed versus precipitation-aged comparison or the role of Cr-depleted L12/L21 precipitates and matrix–precipitate interfaces.
The experiment omits quantitative oxidation mass-gain and scale-growth kinetics, which are necessary to establish improved oxidation resistance rather than merely altered oxide morphology.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses the broad problem and correctly identifies continuity and adhesion of a protective Cr- or Al-rich scale as important to high-temperature oxidation resistance. Its cited evidence gives some support for Mn-dominated nonprotective oxidation in CrMnFeCoNi and for grain refinement plus Y improving scale formation in another alloy. However, it is a different materials hypothesis rather than a reconstruction of the target study. The target concerns one SLM Al-Co-Cr-Fe-Ni-Ti alloy before and after aging, where aging creates Cr-depleted precipitates and extra interfaces that delay protective Cr2O3 formation and modestly increase oxidation. The generated mechanism instead predicts beneficial short-circuit diffusion from nanocrystallinity and beneficial Y additions. Its baseline has the wrong composition and microstructure, and its 700–1100 °C boundary only partially overlaps the target's 600–1200 °C, 96 h domain. The proposed test is also confounded because processing and composition are changed together; a factorial comparison separating grain refinement and Y addition, combined with time-resolved mass gain, scale thickness, spallation, and elemental profiles, would be required. E1 and E2 support parts of the alternative, while E3 concerns V2O5 evaporation in a TiAl-based alloy and offers little direct support.
